analysis.one_liner: Requires the Agriculture Department to set and enforce pathogen limits in raw meat and poultry.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in March 2002 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have told the Secretary of Agriculture to identify the dangerous bacteria in raw meat and poultry, measure how contaminated meat actually is at processing plants, and set limits on contamination that plants must meet using the best available technology. Plants that repeatedly failed and did not fix the problem could no longer stamp their meat 'inspected and passed.' It would also have made clear that the government has the power to enforce these standards, and created a panel of independent scientists to advise on food safety rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who eat meat and poultry. Foodborne bacteria like Salmonella and Campylobacter in raw meat and poultry sicken hundreds of thousands of Americans each year, often through cross-contamination in home kitchens. The bill would have required plants to reduce contamination to levels the best-performing plants already achieve.

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary must prescribe pathogen reduction performance standards for raw meat and poultry that ensure the lowest level of contamination reasonably achievable with the best available technology, using the performance of the best quartile of plants as a benchmark.
The Department must conduct regular microbial testing at plants, and a plant that fails a standard and does not take corrective action can no longer label its products 'inspected and passed.'

The bill explicitly confirms the Secretary's authority to issue and enforce pathogen performance standards and to enforce the standards in effect on January 1, 2000, closing off a challenge based on claimed lack of authority.

The Secretary must publish a list of significant pathogens, run statistically representative contamination surveys and publish the results, and establish an independent National Advisory Committee for Microbiology Criteria for Foods to advise federal food safety agencies.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing plants, which would have to do regular microbial testing, meet contamination limits, and take corrective action or lose the government 'inspected and passed' mark that lets their product move in commerce. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers in slightly higher meat prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on processors and could be passed through to consumers as higher meat prices, an effect felt most by households that spend a large share of their budget on food.

The enforcement tool is comparatively narrow: a failing plant loses the 'inspected and passed' label for affected products rather than facing plant closure, so the bill's direct consequences for persistent violators are limited.

Because the standards must reflect what is 'reasonably achievable' with existing technology, the first standards would be set years after enactment on a staggered timeline, so health benefits would arrive slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health upside is real but gradual: contamination limits benchmarked to the best-performing plants, published survey data, and enforcement teeth would push processors to cut bacteria levels that currently sicken many Americans. The costs are compliance spending by processors and some pass-through to meat prices, and the bill's enforcement remedy (withholding the inspection mark) is a measured one rather than plant closure. A good-faith objection is that most raw meat is cooked before eating, which kills many pathogens; the bill's own findings answer that cross-contamination in kitchens spreads bacteria to other foods and surfaces, so contamination upstream still matters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in March 2002 and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on March 14, 2002, joined by original cosponsors Senators Durbin, Clinton, and Schumer.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
Seven senators cosponsored the bill, six Democrats and one Republican.
No further action was taken: the committee never reported the bill, and there was no floor debate or vote before the Congress ended.

The bill's stated purpose was to protect public health by focusing federal meat and poultry inspection on reducing pathogens at the slaughter and processing stage, where contamination often originates.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors were better off, because they avoided mandatory microbial testing, contamination limits, and the threat of losing the 'inspected and passed' label. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa and chair of the Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Agriculture Committee, which he chaired.

for.name: Richard Durbin, Hillary Clinton, and Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 7 of 100 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no committee or floor vote ever occurred.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.role: Meatpacking and poultry processing companies subject to federal inspection
against.what_they_did: The industry opposed legally enforceable pathogen performance standards and USDA authority to sanction plants that fail microbial testing, an issue it fought in court and in the regulatory process throughout this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to produce a vote, so no roll-call split exists; its sponsors were Democrats plus one Republican cosponsor out of 49 Senate Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have required microbial testing, pathogen reduction standards benchmarked to top-performing plants, and corrective action at slaughter and processing establishments, with failing plants losing the 'inspected and passed' label. Those are real compliance costs, but the industry's interest in avoiding enforceable contamination limits ran against consumers' interest in lower bacteria levels in the meat they buy.

industries.industry: Federal meat and poultry inspection system (USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service)
industries.note: The bill would have expanded the agency's mandate to pathogen testing, surveys, and enforcement, and codified its authority to enforce existing performance standards. Its interest as the public's inspector runs with consumers' health interests.
